clue.text: It gives some idea of what's in store for us

definitions.text: It gives some idea of what's in store for us

parts.words: It gives some idea of what's in store for us
parts.note: 'in store' reads as 'awaiting us in future', but it means literally inside a shop, whose front glass displays its goods

explanation.surface: A fortune-teller's hint about what the future holds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's in store for us' suggests prophecy; read 'store' as a shop, and the thing that shows passers-by its contents is the display behind the front glass.
explanation.definitionFit: A retailer's front display window shows passing customers samples of the goods sold inside.

clue.text: It doesn't necessarily sound derisive

parts.note: hooting can be jeering, but a horn or siren makes the same noise merely as a warning

explanation.surface: Reassurance that some noise was not meant as mockery.
explanation.walkthrough: Hooting at someone is derisive, but a car horn or factory siren hoots without meaning any scorn.
explanation.definitionFit: A horn or siren is a device that makes a loud warning noise, not a jeer.

clue.text: Small payment for working below ground ?

definitions.text: Small payment for working below ground

parts.words: Small payment for working below ground
parts.note: a meagre wage, with the word's start sounding like a coal pit, where miners work underground

explanation.surface: A complaint that miners are poorly paid.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a tiny wage, and its first syllable is a mine shaft, so it is presented as pay for working in one.
explanation.definitionFit: A very small or inadequate sum of money paid to someone.

clue.text: Don Alhambra del Bolero was a grand one

definitions.text: Don Alhambra del Bolero was a grand one

parts.words: Don Alhambra del Bolero was a grand one
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Gondoliers this character holds the title of Grand ... of Spain

explanation.surface: A remark about a character in a comic opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Don Alhambra del Bolero is the Grand Inquisitor in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Gondoliers.
explanation.definitionFit: An official of the Spanish Inquisition who questioned suspected heretics.

clue.text: Maybe Mr. Reade wasn't fancy-free !

indicators.note: 'Maybe' hints that the name could be other letters, so it is rearranged

explanation.surface: Speculation that a man named Reade was in love or lost in imagination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' turns the letters of MR READE into a word for one whose fancy (imagination) is never free, a person lost in reveries.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone given to fantasies and reveries has a mind full of fancies.

clue.text: Sound way to stop a horse

definitions.text: Sound way to stop a horse

parts.words: Sound way to stop a horse
parts.note: 'sound' looks like 'reliable', but it means a noise: the call a rider makes to halt a horse

explanation.surface: Advice on a reliable method of halting a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' reads as an adjective meaning safe; it is a noun, the vocal command used to bring a horse to a stop.
explanation.definitionFit: The command riders and drivers call out to make a horse halt.

clue.text: How one might look if fleeced ?

definitions.text: How one might look if fleeced

parts.words: How one might look if fleeced
parts.note: fleecing is cheating someone out of money, but a fleece also belongs to a woolly farm animal

explanation.surface: A description of the face of someone who has been swindled.
explanation.walkthrough: Someone fleeced (cheated) looks embarrassed; the adjective also means like a woolly flock animal, the one that literally has a fleece.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking embarrassed and awkward, like a meek flock animal.

clue.text: It needn't describe one in rude health

definitions.text: It needn't describe one in rude health

parts.words: It needn't describe one in rude health
parts.note: 'rude health' means robust fitness, but 'rude' alone suggests impoliteness

explanation.surface: A remark that a word does not apply to someone very fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rude health' is vigorous good health, so a robust person need not be impolite, which is what the answer describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Having bad manners; impolite or discourteous.

clue.text: That little 'blankety-blank dash !

parts.note: 'blankety-blank' is a mild curse, but here it is the short stroke joining 'blankety' to 'blank'

explanation.surface: Someone cursing a tiny, annoying punctuation mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blankety-blank' is a euphemism for swearing, so the clue sounds exasperated; the joke is that the little dash it damns is the very mark linking the two halves of that word.
explanation.definitionFit: A short dash that joins two words into one compound, as in 'blankety-blank', is this punctuation mark.

clue.text: Would its 1 be the French kind ?

definitions.text: Would its 1 be the French kind

parts.words: Would its 1 be the French kind
parts.note: the 1 refers to the answer at 1 across, a display window; this outlet's window would be of the French sort because its very name is the French word for a shop

explanation.surface: A wondering question about whether some display is French in style.
explanation.walkthrough: The '1' points to 1 across, SHOP WINDOW. The answer is a French word for a small shop, so its shop window would be a French one.
explanation.definitionFit: A small fashionable store takes its name from the French word for a shop, so its display would be French.

clue.text: An article the parent regarded as a curse?

parts.note: taken as written
A is the indefinite article
taken as written
MA is a mother, a parent

explanation.surface: Someone's mother looked on some object as a jinx.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regarded as' only links the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal ecclesiastical curse of excommunication is the original meaning, hence anything cursed or loathed.

clue.text: A sprint for the river

parts.note: a sprint is a fast run

explanation.surface: A runner dashes towards the river bank.
explanation.walkthrough: The ARUN is a river in Sussex, in southern England, reaching the sea at Littlehampton.
explanation.definitionFit: This Sussex waterway flows south through Arundel to the English Channel.

clue.text: So it's a case perhaps of people getting together

indicators.note: 'perhaps' suggests the letters could form something else, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A speculation about why some people have gathered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges SO IT'S A CASE; 'of' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Partners or colleagues are people who have joined together in some enterprise.

clue.text: Isn't a tenor uncommonly loud-mouthed?

indicators.note: 'uncommonly' says these letters are set out in an unusual order, so the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A question about whether tenors are unusually noisy singers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uncommonly' looks like an intensifier for 'loud-mouthed', but it signals the anagram of ISN'T A TENOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Stentor was a Greek herald in the Iliad whose voice equalled fifty men's, so a booming voice bears his name.

clue.text: Like the short cut that avoids imprisonment?

definitions.text: Like the short cut that avoids imprisonment

parts.words: Like the short cut that avoids imprisonment
parts.note: a quick route reduces the hours spent, and avoiding prison means not having to do a stretch, or serve a sentence

explanation.surface: A remark on a quick route that also dodges a jail term.
explanation.walkthrough: A short cut saves time; avoiding imprisonment also saves 'time', the slang for a prison sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: Reducing the hours needed for something, as a shorter route does.

clue.text: Allotted span, even chez the Empress of Blandings

indicators.note: 'chez' is French for 'at the home of', so one word is lodged inside the creature's home

parts.note: in P. G. Wodehouse's Blandings stories the Empress is Lord Emsworth's prize pig, who lives in a sty
taken as written

explanation.surface: A life's length measured out, even at the home of a famous pig.
explanation.walkthrough: The Empress is a pig, and a pig's home is a STY; 'chez' (at the home of) puts EVEN inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible's Psalm 90 gives a human life as threescore years and ten, the traditional allotted span.

clue.text: " To offer it the show of — " (Hamlet)

definitions.text: To offer it the show of

parts.words: To offer it the show of
parts.note: a line from Hamlet, Act 1 scene 1, where Marcellus says of the Ghost that it is wrong to threaten it with force

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Hamlet with its last word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Marcellus says of the Ghost: 'We do it wrong, being so majestical, To offer it the show of violence.' The answer completes the quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical force or aggression, here a threat made against the Ghost with weapons.

clue.text: Kind of girl to break men's hearts ?

definitions.text: Kind of girl to break men's hearts

parts.words: Kind of girl to break men's hearts
parts.note: a heartbreaker is a stunningly attractive woman, and breaking things is literally smashing them

explanation.surface: A description of a heartbreaking beauty.
explanation.walkthrough: Old British slang calls a gorgeous woman a 'smasher'; the clue plays on the literal sense, one who smashes, here smashing hearts.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a very attractive person, literally one who breaks things to pieces.

clue.text: The non-explosive type at Dunkirk

parts.note: Dunkirk recalls the 1940 evacuation under artillery fire, but it is also a beach where harmless shells lie on the sand

explanation.surface: A recollection of the 1940 evacuation beaches.
explanation.walkthrough: Dunkirk suggests the wartime bombardment of 1940, but it is a seaside town too, and the shells on its beach are the harmless kind left by molluscs.
explanation.definitionFit: The hard outer casing of a mollusc, often found washed up on beaches.

clue.text: Physiotherapist service way back in France

parts.note: Mass is a church service

indicators.note: 'back' says the French word for a street is written in reverse after the church service

parts.note: with 'in France', a way or street is RUE in French

explanation.surface: A French physio whose surgery is behind a church on a street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'way ... in France' is the French RUE, and 'back' turns it to EUR after MASS.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who treats muscles and joints by rubbing and kneading, a form of physical therapy.

clue.text: TV's X

definitions.meaning: a long-running British ITV soap opera set in a Midlands motel
the letter's shape shows two lines meeting and crossing, like two roads

explanation.surface: A cryptic label for some television programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a famous British television soap of that name, and a junction where roads intersect, shaped like the letter.

clue.text: All yours — not ours, chum !

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: 'not' tells us to drop one word's letters from another

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Something offered to a pal: entirely theirs, not ours.
explanation.walkthrough: Take OURS away from YOURS ('not ours') to leave Y, and put it after ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: A friend or supporter on one's side is a chum, a mate.

clue.text: Dancing cavalier ?

parts.note: a mounted soldier armed with a long spear, whose name also gives a square dance

explanation.surface: A horseman who likes to dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lancers is a nineteenth-century quadrille; the singular is a cavalryman armed with a lance.
explanation.definitionFit: A cavalry soldier who carries a long spear; the Lancers is also a set dance.

clue.text: Being in bed, do they mean to change units ?

indicators.note: 'to change' tells us to alter the order of the four letters of the word before it

parts.note: a unit is a one

explanation.surface: Someone in bed wonders whether to switch units of measurement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being in bed' sounds like someone asleep, but the beings are flowers in a garden bed; MEAN changed gives ANEM, then ONES.
explanation.definitionFit: These windflowers are living things grown in flower beds in a garden.

clue.text: Awkward ones in the lobby

indicators.note: 'Awkward' implies something put out of its natural order, so these four letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Troublesome people hanging about in a hotel foyer.
explanation.walkthrough: The lobby is the division lobby of the House of Commons, where MPs voting against a motion file through; 'Awkward' rearranges ONES.
explanation.definitionFit: Votes against a motion, counted as members pass through the parliamentary division lobby.

clue.text: Not what the soldier said, Sam Weller was told

definitions.text: Not what the soldier said, Sam Weller was told

parts.words: Not what the soldier said, Sam Weller was told
parts.note: in Dickens's Pickwick Papers the judge stops Sam Weller quoting a soldier, telling him that hearsay of that kind is inadmissible in court

explanation.surface: A recollection of a scene from Dickens's Pickwick Papers.
explanation.walkthrough: At the trial in Pickwick Papers Sam Weller starts to repeat a soldier's words and the judge cuts in that what the soldier said is not something a court can accept as proof.
explanation.definitionFit: Testimony or proof admissible in court; hearsay such as a soldier's reported words does not count.

clue.text: Outwit at this card game

definitions.meaning: a trick-taking card game for four, popular in nineteenth-century America

explanation.surface: A boast of outsmarting someone at a particular card game.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a trick-taking game with cards, and the verb from that game meaning to gain an advantage over somebody.

clue.text: Upkeep is not their strong point

definitions.text: Upkeep is not their strong point

parts.words: Upkeep is not their strong point
parts.note: 'upkeep' means maintenance, but read as 'keeping up', which laggards fail to do

explanation.surface: A remark about people who neglect maintenance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upkeep' looks like property maintenance; split it as 'keep up', what those falling behind a group cannot do.
explanation.definitionFit: People who lag behind the main group are poor at keeping pace with others.
